attacks.claim: The cost math is per day, not per month. 38M lines x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens/day, which at $0.50/1M is ~$1,140/day, or ~$34k/month. Output is similarly daily (~$7/day, ~$210/month). The stated ~$1,150/month is off by roughly 30x against a $1,500/month budget.
attacks.evidence: "Input: 38M lines x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens -> ~$1,140" and "Estimated total: ~$1,150/month, within the $1,500 budget."

attacks.claim: No spend controls or caps exist for a runaway case. Peak days are 61M lines, and the plan has no token budget, sampling, or per-service throttle to bound spend if log volume spikes during an incident, when volume is highest.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: any spend cap, sampling, or rate limit. Only "peak day 61M" is stated.

attacks.claim: log-tap forwards every application log line with no sampling, backpressure, or bounded queue. At 61M/day peak, or 10-100x growth, the summarizer queue and LLM throughput have no stated limits or rate-limit handling.
attacks.evidence: "forwards every application log line to the summarizer queue"; ABSENT: queue bounds, sampling, or LLM rate-limit strategy.

attacks.claim: Log lines are untrusted input, including attacker-controllable user strings. They are fed to an LLM whose output is posted to the PagerDuty incident and includes a "suspected deploy" field. Prompt injection via log content could mislead responders, and nothing validates or sanitizes the output before it reaches an external integration.
attacks.evidence: "sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service to the LLM with a fixed prompt"; "the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment with the latest summaries"; ABSENT: injection defenses or output validation.

attacks.claim: Redaction covers only emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs. Production logs commonly carry names, customer/tenant identifiers, addresses, and free text. These would reach a third-party LLM and be stored in summaries that are posted to PagerDuty. The privacy claim rests on an audit of an incomplete redaction set and on a zero-retention setting that is asserted, not verified.
attacks.evidence: "already masks emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs"; "Corvid account has zero-retention enabled"; ABSENT: coverage of other PII classes and verification of retention.

attacks.claim: The design is hard-wired to one external vendor with no fallback, no self-hosted option, no stated data residency, and no exit path. A vendor outage or pricing change stops the feature, and migrating prompts and eval baselines is unplanned.
attacks.evidence: "Model: Corvid-mini"; ABSENT: data residency, alternate provider, self-host option, or exit plan.

attacks.claim: Failure handling is unspecified. The plan does not cover LLM timeouts, outages, or rate limits, nor what the PagerDuty comment shows when summaries are stale or missing. There is no alerting on the summarizer, so it can fail silently during the incidents it is meant to help.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retry policy, timeout values, fallback behavior, summarizer health alerts, or stale-summary handling. Only "Hardening, dashboards, runbook" is listed.

attacks.claim: The 5-minute batch cadence contradicts the "within seconds of a page" goal. The summary attached at page time can be up to 5 minutes old, plus LLM latency, and may predate the incident start. The "suspected deploy" field has no specified deploy data source.
attacks.evidence: "every 5 minutes, sends the last 5 minutes of logs" vs "within seconds of a page"; "suspected deploy" with no source named.

attacks.claim: The core value claim is unsupported. The 47 -> 30 minute MTTR target has no baseline attribution or causal mechanism. The 15-20 minute grep-time figure is not measured. The eval measures summary quality, not MTTR impact.
attacks.evidence: "instead of spending the first 15-20 minutes grepping logs"; "Target: median MTTR 47 min -> 30 min"; eval grades usefulness only.

attacks.claim: The launch gate rests on 40 historical incidents, which is a small sample. At 5% misleading, that is 2 of 40. The prompt may also be tuned on the same incidents, so the gate may overfit. No grader agreement is measured.
attacks.evidence: "Launch gate: >= 70% useful, <= 5% misleading"; "Eval set from last 40 incidents".

attacks.claim: The staffing math ignores the stated 50% on-call load. Two engineers at 100% for 6 weeks give 12 eng-weeks, but half their time is already consumed by on-call. Realistic capacity is ~6 eng-weeks, so the plan has zero slack and is infeasible as scheduled.
attacks.evidence: "on-call/interrupt work averages 50% of their time"; "both platform engineers full-time for 6 weeks (2 x 6 = 12 eng-weeks)".

attacks.claim: Summary relevance depends on the service catalog for direct dependencies. A stale catalog would produce wrong or missing dependency summaries, and this coupling is not addressed in the plan.
attacks.evidence: "direct dependencies (from the service catalog)"; ABSENT: catalog freshness or validation.

attacks.claim: log-tap is inserted into the existing Vector pipeline, but no feature flag or rollback path is described. Removing or changing the tap mid-incident is not addressed.
attacks.evidence: "log-tap (new): subscribes to the existing Vector pipeline after the redaction stage"; ABSENT: rollback or kill switch.

attacks.claim: Sending production logs to an external LLM may conflict with customer contract terms on subprocessors or data sharing. The DPA covers the vendor, but customer-level terms are not checked.
attacks.evidence: "data processing addendum signed by Legal (ref DPA-0417)"; ABSENT: customer contract or subprocessor review.

attacks.claim: The plan assumes responders need LLM summaries of logs. It does not show that on-call engineers lack a faster signal, such as existing dashboards or traces.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: user research or responder feedback on current triage pain.

attacks.claim: No material ui finding. The only surface is an auto-comment in PagerDuty, and the plan does not specify its format.
attacks.evidence: "the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment with the latest summaries".

attacks.claim: No material accessibility finding. The output is plain-text summaries in an existing tool, though the plan does not state formatting or language constraints.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: output format spec.

attacks.claim: The cost math treats a daily volume as monthly. 38M lines/day x 60 tokens is 2.28B tokens per day, which is about $1,140 per day and roughly $34k per month at $0.50/1M, about 23x the $1,500 budget. The artifact's '~$1,150/month' figure is off by about 30x.
attacks.evidence: "Input: 38M lines x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens -> ~$1,140" alongside "38M lines/day average" and "Estimated total: ~$1,150/month, within the $1,500 budget."

attacks.claim: Even with the corrected volume, the estimate omits the fixed prompt overhead sent on each of the 8,640 calls per day, and it ignores the 61M-line peak-day case. Budget headroom is not analysed.
attacks.evidence: "Input: 38M lines x 60 tokens" (no prompt tokens counted) and "peak day 61M" (no cost at peak)

attacks.claim: log-tap is inserted into the shared Vector pipeline with no described backpressure, buffering, or drop policy. If the summarizer queue or the vendor API slows, the risk is stalled or dropped application log shipping, which would affect every consumer of the logs, not only the copilot.
attacks.evidence: "log-tap (new): subscribes to the existing Vector pipeline after the redaction stage and forwards every application log line to the summarizer queue."

attacks.claim: No failure modes, timeouts, retries, or alerting are specified for the 5-minute summarizer loop or for the PagerDuty auto-comment path. On-call could receive stale or missing summaries without knowing it.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retry, timeout, staleness indicator, or alerting for summarizer and PagerDuty comment failures

attacks.claim: The goal of a summary 'within seconds of a page' conflicts with the design, where summaries are generated only every 5 minutes. The summary attached at page time can be up to 5 minutes old plus LLM latency.
attacks.evidence: "within seconds of a page" vs "every 5 minutes, sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service"

attacks.claim: Staffing is infeasible as written. Both engineers are assigned full-time for 6 weeks (12 eng-weeks), yet the charter says on-call and interrupt work averages 50% of their time. The estimate has no slack and no on-call allocation.
attacks.evidence: "Staffing: both platform engineers full-time for 6 weeks (2 x 6 = 12 eng-weeks)." alongside "on-call/interrupt work averages 50% of their time" (context)

attacks.claim: Log lines are attacker-influenced untrusted input (for example user-agent, query strings, error messages). They are fed to an LLM whose output is auto-posted into PagerDuty incidents and used to suggest a deploy. Prompt injection could steer on-call toward a false root cause. The plan has no input sanitisation or output validation.
attacks.evidence: "stores a structured summary (top errors, new error signatures, affected endpoints, suspected deploy)" and "the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment with the latest summaries"

attacks.claim: The privacy argument rests on a redaction stage that masks only emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs. Production logs commonly contain other personal data (names, account IDs, free-text user content, addresses). The plan does not show that these are absent, yet it sends the full log stream to a third party.
attacks.evidence: "already masks emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs for our log retention policy (audited in Q1)"

attacks.claim: The design is hard-wired to a single external vendor and model with no fallback, no self-hosted option, no stated data residency, and no exit plan. Summary prompts and output schemas would also need rework to change vendor.
attacks.evidence: "Model: Corvid-mini" and ABSENT: fallback provider, self-hosting option, data residency region, or migration path

attacks.claim: Sending production logs to a new subprocessor may require customer notice or contract updates. The plan cites only an internal DPA and does not address whether the log contents contain customer data covered by customer contracts.
attacks.evidence: "Corvid account has zero-retention enabled; data processing addendum signed by Legal (ref DPA-0417)."

attacks.claim: The headline MTTR outcome (47 to 30 min) and the 15-20 minute grep-time saving are unsupported. No prototype, pilot, or measurement of summary usefulness on live incidents precedes the 6-week build commitment.
attacks.evidence: "Target: median MTTR 47 min -> 30 min within one quarter of launch." and ABSENT: prototype or pilot results

attacks.claim: The replay evaluation depends on log retention covering the last 40 incidents, which is not stated. Grading by the incident commander who handled the incident also risks hindsight bias and self-grading.
attacks.evidence: "replay the last 40 incidents ... have the incident commander grade it" with ABSENT: log retention period for replay

attacks.claim: The queue and storage are called negligible without sizing. Forwarding every line (61M/day at peak) into Redis could be significant in memory and throughput terms.
attacks.evidence: "Queue + storage: existing Redis and Postgres, negligible."

attacks.claim: No kill switch or rollback for the auto-comment or the log-tap subscription is described. The plan says summaries are advisory, but disabling the feature safely is not specified.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: disable or rollback procedure for log-tap and PagerDuty auto-comments

attacks.claim: Nothing gate-worthy found beyond the PagerDuty auto-comment format, which is unspecified.
attacks.evidence: "the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment with the latest summaries"

attacks.claim: Nothing gate-worthy found. Posting an extra comment on each page may add noise, but this is not a gate blocker.
attacks.evidence: "the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment"

attacks.claim: Nothing gate-worthy found. The plan does not mention output format for screen readers, but the output is text.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: accessibility considerations (none gate-worthy)

attacks.claim: The value of plain-language summaries over existing dashboards is asserted rather than shown. Value depends on summary accuracy, which has not been tested.
attacks.evidence: "Give the on-call engineer a plain-language 'what is going wrong right now' summary"

attacks.claim: The dependency on service catalog accuracy for 'direct dependencies' is unverified, and the integration is allotted only 2 weeks.
attacks.evidence: "PagerDuty integration + service catalog | 2"

attacks.claim: The cost math mixes daily and monthly figures. 38M lines/day x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens/day, which is about $1,140/day, or roughly $34k/month at $0.50/1M, not $1,140/month. Output is also understated: 3.5M tokens/day at $2/1M is about $7/day, or about $207/month. The real total is roughly 23x the $1,500 budget, and the plan has no spend cap or kill switch.
attacks.evidence: "Input: 38M lines x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens -> ~$1,140" and "Estimated total: ~$1,150/month, within the $1,500 budget."

attacks.claim: Peak-day volume (61M lines) and the fixed per-call prompt overhead across 8,640 calls/day are not budgeted, so the estimate is a floor even after correcting the daily/monthly error.
attacks.evidence: "Application logs: 38M lines/day average across 30 services (peak day 61M)." ABSENT: prompt token overhead per call and peak-day cost.

attacks.claim: Average window size is about 4,400 lines per service per 5-minute call (38M / 30 / 288), or roughly 264k input tokens per request. Peak is about 423k tokens. That likely exceeds model context and per-request limits, and the plan has no chunking, truncation, or sampling strategy.
attacks.evidence: "every 5 minutes, sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service to the LLM with a fixed prompt" and "~60 tokens after redaction." ABSENT: context-limit handling.

attacks.claim: Sustained input is about 26k tokens/s on average, with no rate-limit, concurrency, or quota analysis. At 10-100x growth, the 5-minute batch design and the log-tap queue are unbounded.
attacks.evidence: "log-tap (new): subscribes to the existing Vector pipeline ... and forwards every application log line to the summarizer queue." ABSENT: queue bounds, backpressure, rate-limit plan.

attacks.claim: The plan has no failure-mode, timeout, retry, or alerting design for the summarizer or log-tap. A silent summarizer outage would leave on-call engineers with stale or missing summaries and no signal that they are stale.
attacks.evidence: "Hardening, dashboards, runbook | 2" is the only reliability item. ABSENT: alerts on summarizer lag or failure, LLM timeout/retry policy.

attacks.claim: log-tap sits on the production Vector log pipeline. If the summarizer queue or Redis backs up, the plan does not say whether Vector is blocked or dropping lines, so the change could degrade the primary logging path that on-call depends on.
attacks.evidence: "subscribes to the existing Vector pipeline after the redaction stage and forwards every application log line to the summarizer queue." ABSENT: backpressure and isolation design.

attacks.claim: The 5-minute cadence and the goal of a summary 'within seconds of a page' conflict. A page can fire up to 5 minutes after the relevant window started, and the on-page comment uses the 'latest summaries', which may predate the incident.
attacks.evidence: "Give the on-call engineer a plain-language 'what is going wrong right now' summary within seconds of a page" vs "every 5 minutes".

attacks.claim: 'New error signatures' and 'suspected deploy' require cross-window state and a deploy-correlation source that the plan never specifies. Service-catalog accuracy for 'direct dependencies' is also assumed, not verified.
attacks.evidence: "stores a structured summary (top errors, new error signatures, affected endpoints, suspected deploy)" and "from the service catalog". ABSENT: state design and deploy-data source.

attacks.claim: The 30-minute MTTR target and the 15-20 minute grep-time saving are asserted without a baseline breakdown or a link to tool impact. The launch gate uses a 40-incident replay graded by the IC. With n=40, '<=5% misleading' allows at most 2 misleading summaries, which is weak evidence.
attacks.evidence: "Target: median MTTR 47 min -> 30 min within one quarter of launch." and "Launch gate: >= 70% useful, <= 5% misleading."

attacks.claim: The model price ($0.50/$2.00 per 1M tokens) and the Corvid-mini quality for log summarization are unsourced and unprototyped. Pricing and quality drive the whole design.
attacks.evidence: "Model: Corvid-mini, $0.50 per 1M input tokens, $2.00 per 1M output tokens." ABSENT: pricing source and model eval results.

attacks.claim: The redaction stage masks only emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs. Logs commonly contain names, user IDs, free-text customer data, and other identifiers that would then leave the perimeter. The plan treats the redaction list as sufficient without checking coverage against the full log content.
attacks.evidence: "already masks emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs for our log retention policy (audited in Q1)." ABSENT: coverage analysis for other personal data.

attacks.claim: The plan creates new stores (Redis queue, Postgres summaries) with no stated retention, access control, or deletion policy. Summaries can echo sensitive log content, and forwarding 'every application log line' expands collection beyond the existing retention policy.
attacks.evidence: "stores a structured summary" and "forwards every application log line to the summarizer queue." ABSENT: retention and access policy for the queue and summaries.

attacks.claim: Single-provider dependency on Corvid with a prompt tuned to one model. There is no fallback, no self-hosted option, and no exit plan. Data residency for the Corvid endpoint is not stated.
attacks.evidence: "Model: Corvid-mini" and "Corvid account has zero-retention enabled". ABSENT: fallback provider, residency region, exit plan.

attacks.claim: Sending production logs, which may contain B2B customer data, to a third-party LLM may require customer contract or subprocessor notice. The plan cites only an internal DPA and does not address customer-facing obligations.
attacks.evidence: "data processing addendum signed by Legal (ref DPA-0417)." ABSENT: customer contract and subprocessor review.

attacks.claim: Log content is attacker-influenced (for example, reflected user input). Passing it to an LLM whose output is auto-posted into the PagerDuty incident creates prompt-injection risk that could mislead responders. The plan has no input-sanitization or output-validation step, and no API-key handling is described.
attacks.evidence: "On page: the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment with the latest summaries". ABSENT: prompt-injection mitigation and key management.

attacks.claim: Advisory-only design is good, but there is no feature flag or documented disable path for the PagerDuty comment or the summarizer. Rollback is not described.
attacks.evidence: "Summaries are advisory only. Alert rules, paging, and escalation policies are unchanged." ABSENT: kill switch and rollback steps.

attacks.claim: Redaction guarantees depend on the position of the Vector redaction stage. A config change upstream could silently change what log-tap sees, creating hidden coupling.
attacks.evidence: "log-tap reads only after the Vector redaction stage". ABSENT: test or contract guarding the redaction position.

attacks.claim: A 5-minute refresh plus a PagerDuty comment may add friction. The plan does not show that responders will check the summaries during an incident.
attacks.evidence: "the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment with the latest summaries". ABSENT: responder workflow evidence.

attacks.claim: The plan assumes plain-language summaries solve the grep problem, but does not test whether the on-call engineer's real bottleneck is grepping or diagnosis.
attacks.evidence: "instead of spending the first 15-20 minutes grepping logs across 30 services". ABSENT: user research or incident-timeline breakdown.

attacks.claim: Nothing substantive: output is text in PagerDuty comments with no custom UI or motion.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no UI component described; output is plain text.

attacks.claim: Nothing substantive: no rendering or layout changes are proposed beyond a PagerDuty text comment.
attacks.evidence: "the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment with the latest summaries".

attacks.claim: Staffing is planned at 12 full-time eng-weeks, but the charter says on-call and interrupt work averages 50% of engineer time. Real capacity is about 6 eng-weeks, so the 6-week schedule is roughly 2x optimistic, with no contingency.
attacks.evidence: "Staffing: both platform engineers full-time for 6 weeks (2 x 6 = 12 eng-weeks)." and the context stating on-call/interrupt work averages 50% of time.
